claims.text: An industrial system has three parts: inputs are what goes in (raw materials, labour, energy and capital), processes are what happens inside (the making, heating and assembling that change raw materials into products), and outputs are what comes out: the products the system sells and the waste it creates.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Processing means changing a raw material into a new product, and the change is what makes it processing: clay becomes bricks, pilchards become canned fish. The test for any flow is whether it goes into the factory or comes out of it, and the flows balance: what enters leaves again, as product or as waste.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A fish cannery shows the system in figures: roughly 40 000 tonnes of fish a year enter as an input, and about 32 000 tonnes leave as canned product and 8 000 tonnes as waste, so four fifths of the intake by mass becomes product and one fifth waste.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Location factors each have a direction: a bulk-losing industry such as copper smelting or cement sits beside its raw material, because most of the mass is discarded in processing; a bakery sits near its market, because loaves are bulkier and more perishable than flour; a footloose industry using light components may prefer a motorway junction or a city with skilled workers.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The full list of location factors is raw materials, labour, energy supply, transport routes, markets, flat land and government policy, and policy can tip the balance: tax breaks and serviced estates have drawn industry to particular towns.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A location question asks why the factory is here, not what it does here: jobs created, noise and dust are impacts, and answering a location question with impacts answers a different question. An industrial case study is a named factory or zone small enough to be marked on a town map, not a whole country.

claims.text: The Ohorongo cement works stands near Otavi, a town on Namibia's north-south railway in the Otjozondjupa region; production began in 2011 after an investment of about N$2.5 billion, the works employs around 300 permanent workers (2010s figure), and its marble-rich rock is cut at a quarry beside the site.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Ohorongo is located near Otavi because cement is bulk-losing, so the works sits at the quarry rather than hauling rock; Otavi's railway junction brings fuel and equipment in and takes cement out; the town supplies labour, water and services; and northern Namibia's building market lies close by, so the heavy finished product travels short distances.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The works as a system: inputs of quarry rock, fuel, electricity, water and labour; processes of crushing, grinding, burning in kilns and grinding again with additives; outputs of bagged and bulk cement, plus kiln gases, dust and warm air as waste streams.
